title: Gray failure and detection latency
summary: The failure mode that breaks real fleets is a replica that reports healthy while serving at a fraction of its speed, because load balancers keep sending it work.

steps.title: A healthy fleet, before anything happens
body: Two hundred and fifty-six replicas ready, none ejected, p2c routing at 560 requests a second against a rated 1878. Every replica is announcing healthy and every replica is in fact healthy: SLO attainment is 97 percent and TTFT p99 is 3.4 seconds.
The scripted failure schedule fires at t=60 s. Watch the ready count: it will not change, in either run.
steps.look_for: The counters, and the empty failure-events panel.

steps.title: Replica 5 is now serving at 0.3x, and says it is fine
body: Health is a vector, not a boolean. The announced state is still healthy, because nothing crashed; the true speed multiplier is 0.3, which the simulator knows and no policy does.

p2c compares in-flight counts, and in-flight counts equalise: a replica that finishes slowly is sent less only in proportion to its slowness, never nothing. Every request it gets is slow. The one tell in the delayed view is its step time, 34 ms decoding where the fleet median is 11, and 156 ms when it carries a prefill chunk where a healthy replica takes 48.
steps.look_for: The ready count still at 256, while the machine tab's step-time column has grown one outlier.

steps.title: What the inference would look like
body: Sort the table by step time, descending. One replica sits at three to fourteen times the others, depending on whether the view caught it decoding or prefilling. That is the signal a detection policy has to act on, and everything else in the fleet looks normal.

It is a blunt signal. A healthy replica's step time is bimodal, 11 ms decoding and 48 ms carrying a 1024-token prefill chunk, a 4.4x spread inside one healthy fleet. A detector that ejects at three times the median ejected half of this fleet by t=20 s in a run with no failure at all. Eight times the median separates the two, and the price is that the gray replica's decode-only views, at three times, look healthy.
steps.look_for: The outlier row, and how little else distinguishes it from a replica that is merely mid-prefill.

steps.title: Detected, and ejected, 4.3 seconds late
body: In the compared run the outlier policy ejected replica 5 at t=64.3 s: three consecutive one-second views above eight times the fleet median, each delivered 200 ms late. During those 4.3 seconds the router kept sending it work, and every one of those requests missed its SLO.

Detection latency is the number to optimise here, and it trades directly against false positives: eject a replica that was merely carrying a long prefill and you have removed capacity from a fleet that needed it. Here the view count and the ratio are the two knobs, and both were set by measuring the healthy spread first.
steps.look_for: The ejected counter at one in the compared run, and at zero in this one.

steps.title: Thirty seconds out, then judged again
body: The cooldown ended at t=94.3 s and the replica was re-admitted with a clean record. It was still at 0.3x, and three fresh views later, at t=100.3 s, it was out again. A cooldown is a re-assessment, not a pardon.

The fleet-level numbers barely move, because one replica is 0.4 percent of 256: SLO attainment 97.1 percent in both runs, TTFT p99 3355 ms without ejection against 3322 with, no timeouts in either. The difference lives on the replica: 49 requests reached it after the onset without detection and 48 of them missed their SLO; with ejection 20 reached it, all before detection or during the re-admission window, and all 20 missed. Fleet-wide, 883 SLO misses after t=60 became 853.
steps.look_for: The SLO attainment line, and how a 1-in-256 failure hides inside it.
